ARGUMENTS AND FINDINGS 6.

The golden principles to be followed in a case based on circumstantial evidence have been laid down in the celebrated judgment passed by Hon'ble Apex Court in Sharad Birdi Chand Sharda Vs.
State of Maharashtra AIR 1984 SC 1622 that are as under :-
A close analysis of this decision would show that the following conditions must be fulfilled before a case against an accused can be said to be fully established:

sentences.text: (1) the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established.

It may be noted here that this Court indicated that the circumstances concerned 'must or should'
and not 'may be' established.

There is not only a grammatical but a legal distinction between 'may be proved' and 'must be or should be proved' as was held by this Court in Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade &
Anr. v. State of Maharashtra(') where the following observations were made:
"Certainly, it is a primary principle that the accused must be and not merely may be guilty before a court can convict and the mental distance between 'may be' and 'must be' is long and divides vague conjectures from sure conclusions."

It is argued that the complainant/PW-1 and his wife/PW-6 have made general allegations of taunting by the accused which do not constitute an offence u/s 498A IPC or u/s 304B IPC.
It is argued that the necessary ingredients of the charges have not been proved on record and the accused is entitled to be acquitted.
15. On behalf of the State, it is argued that PW-1 & PW-6 categorically deposed that the accused used to taunt the deceased on several issues.
Due to the continuous taunting by the accused, the deceased was driven to commit suicide within 5 years 3 months of her marriage.

Section 498A IPC provides as under :-
Section 498A IPC. Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty.--Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman,
subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.--

For the purpose of this section, "cruelty" means-- (a) any wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on State Vs. sentences.text: 16. Neither PW-1 nor PW-6 alleged that there was any demand for any property/dowry at the time or after the marriage.
Therefore, the case is not covered under explanation (b) of Section 498A IPC.
To bring out a case of cruelty under explanation (a), it must be shown that there was a willful conduct which was of such a nature as is likely to drive a woman to commit suicide.
General taunting or nagging cannot be treated as such conduct unless it is of such a nature so as to drive the woman to commit suicide.
In the case in hand, PW-1 & PW-6 deposed the instances of taunting wherein the accused stated that the accused has treated their daughter badly and she was beaten mercilessly.
The question before the court is whether such instances of taunting can be considered as being of such a nature so as to drive Neetu to commit suicide.
The alleged tauntings are more in the form of complaints that are usually made in the families.
They are not of such a nature as would drive Neetu to commit suicide.

It is a fact that Neetu had committed suicide but connecting the said suicide with the aforesaid general tauntings will be too much of imagination and is more of a suspicion of parents, who have lost their daughter.
However, the suspicion, howsoever grave, cannot take place of proof.
In a criminal case, the standard of proof is beyond reasonable doubts and not preponderance of probabilities.
State Vs. Harvinder Dalal & Ors.
FIR No.201/15 Page no.20 of 22 State vs. Harvinder Dalal & Ors.

17. After taking into account the nature of the comments/taunting, I am of the view that the same are manifestly falling short of cruelty within the meaning of explanation (a) of the Section 498A IPC.
18.
Besides the above instances of general taunting, there is no further material on record to prove the charge u/s 498A IPC.

The evidence available on record is highly insufficient to bring home guilt u/s 498A IPC.
19.
I will now examine the charge u/s 304B IPC.

Section 304B provides as under:-
Section 304B. Dowry death.

-- (1) Where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for,
or in connection with, any demand for dowry, such death shall be called "dowry death", and such husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused her death.

Explanation - For the purposes of this sub-section, "dowry" shall have the same meaning as in section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 (28 of 1961).
Whoever commits dowry death shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years but which may extend to imprisonment for life.]
20. U/S 113 B of the Indian Evidence Act, a presumption of having caused the dowry death can be raised only if it is shown that soon before her death, such woman has been subjected by the accused to cruelty or harassment for, or in connection with any demand for dowry.

On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel argued that the said annoyance, even if presumed to be true, cannot be treated as a dowry demand.

23. Hence, on the basis of the material available on record and evidence led by the side of the prosecution, this Court has no hesitation in holding that the prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond all reasonable doubts.
24. For want of sufficient evidence, the charges could not be proved against the accused.
CONCLUSION 25.
In view of the foregoing discussion, the accused Harvinder is found not guilty and is accordingly acquitted of the charges under Section 498A IPC & Section 304B IPC framed against him.
